blocks.heading: Sets and elements
blocks.text: A set is a collection of distinct objects. Its objects are called elements. A = {1, 2, 3}. The notation 2 ∈ A means “2 is an element of A.” Listing an element twice does not create a new element.

blocks.heading: Natural numbers
blocks.text: In the convention used here, the natural numbers are {0, 1, 2, 3, …}. Some texts start at 1, so always check the stated convention or the problem’s starting value.

blocks.heading: Roster method
blocks.text: The roster method lists the elements between braces, separated by commas. A = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5}. Order does not matter: {1, 2} = {2, 1}.

blocks.heading: Set-builder notation
blocks.text: Set-builder notation describes a property that elements must satisfy. {x | condition on x} B = {x | x is an even integer and x < 10}. Without a lower bound, B also contains negative even integers.

blocks.heading: Interval notation
blocks.text: Interval notation describes sets of real numbers. Parentheses exclude endpoints; square brackets include them. Infinity is never an included endpoint. (1, 5): 1 < x < 5. [2, 6]: 2 ≤ x ≤ 6. (−∞, 3]: x ≤ 3.

blocks.heading: Union
blocks.text: The union, A ∪ B, contains elements in A, in B, or in both. A = {1, 3, 5}; B = {1, 2, 6}. A ∪ B = {1, 2, 3, 5, 6}. In a Venn diagram, union includes both circles, not just their overlap.

blocks.heading: Intersection
blocks.text: The intersection, A ∩ B, contains only shared elements. A = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5}. B = {3, 4, 6, 9, 12}. A ∩ B = {3, 4}. The overlapping region of a Venn diagram represents intersection.

blocks.heading: Set difference
blocks.text: The difference, A − B, contains elements of A that are not in B. The order matters. X = {a, b, c, d, e}; Y = {a, c, f, g}. X − Y = {b, d, e}. Y − X = {f, g}.

blocks.heading: Empty, finite, and infinite sets
blocks.text: The empty set has no elements: ∅ or {}. A finite set has a finite number of elements, such as {1, 2, 3, 4, 5}. An infinite set has infinitely many elements, such as {1, 2, 3, …}.

blocks.heading: Universal set
blocks.text: The universal set, U, contains all elements under discussion. U = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8}. A = {4, 6, 7, 8}; B = {1, 2, 3, 7, 8}. A and B are both subsets of this U.

blocks.heading: Subsets
blocks.text: A subset has every element in another set. X ⊆ Y allows equality. A proper subset, X ⊂ Y, is a subset unequal to Y. X = {10, 20, 30}. Y = {10, 20, 30, 40}. Then X ⊂ Y.

blocks.heading: Complements
blocks.text: The complement of A within U is A^c = U − A. It contains elements in U but outside A. U = {2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12}. A = {2, 4, 6}. A^c = {8, 10, 12}. A complement is always relative to a specified universal set.
